tier_reason: The only numbers are an ad-hoc Ruby Benchmark.bmbm run (benchmark/idna.rb) in an open, unmerged third-party PR to the addressable gem; the script is public and checks each backend's to_ascii output against the expected string, but no hardware, OS, Ruby version, compiler or flags are given and it is not a well-known independent suite, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Ruby Benchmark.bmbm output in benchmark/idna.rb, 100,000 to_ascii+to_unicode round trips of one domain. Rehearsal real time: pure Ruby 5.915326 s, libidn 0.522676 s, libidn2 0.763983 s. Measured pass real time: pure Ruby 6.043252 s, libidn 0.521704 s, libidn2 0.764863 s. libidn about 1.47x faster than libidn2 and about 11.6x faster than pure Ruby on the measured pass (derived from page data; 1.46x and 11.3x on the rehearsal). The PR author calls libidn2 'slightly slower than libidn1 as it's doing more work but nothing to worry about, we're still above 100k iterations/sec'.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 3 stars and 2 forks on the GitLab mirror (GitLab API); GNU library packaged by Linux distributions, though the GNU project now steers new users to libidn2
corrections.caveats: One input string, wall time through Ruby binding layers rather than raw C calls, and the bindings are not equivalent: libidn (v1) is called through the idn-ruby gem's native C extension, while libidn2 goes through a new Ruby FFI binding that allocates MemoryPointers per call, so part of the 1.47x gap is binding overhead, not library speed. The two libraries also implement different standards: libidn implements the superseded IDNA2003 (Unicode 3.2 nameprep) while libidn2 implements IDNA2008 plus UTS#46, which the PR author says does more work; libidn's own README warns that IDNA2003 is superseded and asks users to migrate to libidn2. No hardware, OS, Ruby version or compiler stated, and the PR (opened 2023-03-22 by jarthod, branch jarthod/addressable:libidn2) is still open and unmerged. The libidn1 vs libidn2 gap is an incidental side result of a wrapper benchmark, not a claim by the libidn project, whose README makes no performance claim. libidn2's own merge request 134 ('punycode decode: slightly faster for common cases', up to 5 percent) compares libidn2 against itself.

notes: Numbers on the PR page match the record (rehearsal row) and the script verifies all three backends produce the expected ACE string, so the evidence is valid but weak. Shortcomings to record: unequal bindings (native extension vs per-call FFI) confound the 1.47x libidn-over-libidn2 gap; libidn implements the superseded IDNA2003, so it is faster partly by doing less and is deprecated by its own maintainers in favour of the baseline; single string, no hardware or toolchain, unmerged third-party PR.
